tldr: The authors propose GenGenIK, an inverse kinematics method that handles mobile bases, bimanual arms, cluttered obstacle environments, and behavioral preferences within a single Transformer, rapidly sampling high-quality joint trajectories.
hero_caption: Representative application scenarios for GenGenIK. Across diverse tasks that coordinate mobile bases and multi-joint arms—such as grasping objects under tables, handling partially observed environments from a single depth image, and navigating cluttered kitchens with furniture and obstacles—it generates whole-body configurations that avoid environmental collisions.
overview:
When a robot performs tasks like "grasping a cup on a table" or "turning a doorknob," a higher-level planner issues commands as target end-effector poses (positions and orientations). Upon receiving them, the robot must calculate the angles to bend each of its joints. This is inverse kinematics (IK). However, for bimanual robots with multiple end-effectors or robots with mobile bases, the degrees of freedom are very high, meaning countless configurations can realize the same end-effector pose. Traditional numerical IK solvers excel at finding a single solution. But when trying to collect a diverse set of solutions that avoid obstacles or anticipate subsequent continuous motions, they must re-run optimization repeatedly from different initializations, which takes a lot of time.

To solve this, the authors redefine IK as a conditional generative problem. Combining Flow Matching—a technique drawing attention in recent image generation—with Transformers, they developed GenGenIK. It is a framework that learns the entire distribution of feasible joint-space configurations and trajectories, conditioned not only on target end-effector poses, but also on 3D scene point clouds and user preferences such as "keeping elbows high" or "minimizing base movement."

In experiments, the authors evaluated static end-effector targeting, continuous trajectory IK like door opening and bimanual lifting, and collision avoidance under partially observed point clouds using a mobile bimanual robot (Rainbow RB-Y1) and a humanoid robot (Unitree G1). As a result, they demonstrated that GenGenIK speeds up the time to find a first valid solution by up to 34x compared to cuRobo, a GPU-parallelized numerical optimization solver, efficiently sampling valid configurations that connect smoothly to subsequent tasks.
contributions: Proposed a masking representation that unifies mobile bases, multiple end-effectors, multi-target continuous trajectories, and partial joint fixing within a single Transformer architecture.
Constructed a flow model that focuses pose sampling into collision-free regions of the solution space by directly conditioning on 3D scene point clouds.

Combined test-time guidance—which projects differentiable constraints (such as manipulability and static stability) onto the constraint tangent space—with token conditioning for non-differentiable preferences.
Substantially increased the rate at which the initial configuration in trajectory IK allows executing the entire subsequent path, achieving up to a 34x speedup over numerical optimization solvers.

sections.heading: Why We Need "Generalized IK" Beyond Simple End-Effector Matching
sections.summary: Motion planning for high-DoF robots demands diverse whole-body configurations that satisfy countless simultaneous constraints—such as collision avoidance, self-collision prevention, camera visibility, and stability—not just reaching end-effector positions. Because traditional numerical methods that seek a single solution search slowly, this paper introduces GenGenIK, reframing IK as a conditional interpolation generation problem in C-space.
sections.details:
Many robotic tasks are intuitively described in Cartesian task space. However, safety verification and real-robot control require concrete values in the robot's configuration space (C-space). For redundant robots whose degrees of freedom exceed the task-space dimension, countless joint configurations can satisfy the same end-effector pose, so IK is typically solved via non-linear optimization.

Yet, for long-horizon manipulation planning, returning just a single solution is insufficient. For instance, when "reaching deep into a cabinet" or "lifting a heavy object with both hands," the robot must satisfy diverse criteria: where to park the mobile base, whether the hands remain within camera view, whether the robot stays balanced, and whether collisions occur along the way. With conventional numerical solvers, obtaining multiple candidates requires running optimizations repeatedly from different initial values, creating a major computational bottleneck.

To address this, this work proposes "Generalized IK," generating configuration trajectories that simultaneously satisfy multiple end-effectors, mobile bases, obstacle point clouds, and behavioral preferences (such as high manipulability). To solve it, the authors introduce a Transformer-based generative model called GenGenIK, using a masking mechanism to handle everything from single-pose queries to trajectory interpolation within the same network.

captions.F1: Three typical problem settings where GenGenIK excels: reaching under low, confined tables; reaching under incomplete point cloud observations; and avoiding collisions in cluttered kitchens—all flexibly solved by a single unified model.

sections.heading: The Evolution from Analytical and Optimization Solvers to Generative Models
sections.summary: This section surveys existing approaches, including classical analytical methods (IKFast), GPU-accelerated numerical optimization (cuRobo), normalizing flow-based generative IK (IKFlow), and diffusion models (IKDiffuser). GenGenIK unifies and extends these, serving as a new generative solver that encompasses scene awareness, continuous path constraints, mobile bases, and behavioral preferences.
sections.details:
This section organizes the history of IK research into three lineages to clarify GenGenIK's advantages.

### Classical IK and Numerical Solvers
Analytical solvers like IKFast can enumerate solutions quickly, but they depend on specific kinematic structures, and excess redundant degrees of freedom can only be handled through parameter sweeps. On the other hand, modern numerical optimization solvers like Drake and cuRobo flexibly handle self-collisions, environmental collisions, and whole-body configuration costs. However, obtaining a diverse set of solutions requires running optimizations over and over from different initializations.

### Accelerating IK with Generative Models
Generative IK amortizes this repetitive optimization cost through pre-training. IKFlow uses normalizing flows to sample diverse solutions instantaneously, and IKDiffuser uses diffusion models to support multiple end-effectors and differentiable preferences. Nonetheless, most of these methods primarily target single-target points (point IK) in obstacle-free free space.

### Scene-Aware and Path-Constrained IK
Recent works have also incorporated vision (ViIK) or considered entire trajectories (CppFlow, IKLink). GenGenIK integrates the strengths of these prior studies, realizing scene point cloud conditioning, mobile bases, multiple end-effectors, continuous trajectory constraints, and behavioral preferences within a single framework.

sections.heading: Unified Problem Formulation: From Single Poses to Continuous Paths via Masking
sections.summary: Generalized IK is formulated as a conditional generative problem that samples feasible joint trajectories given target pose sequences, scene point clouds, and task masks. Switching masks allows single-target, multi-target, bimanual, and partially fixed configurations to share a common interface.
sections.details:
Let the robot's configuration space be $\mathcal{Q}_R$, the number of end-effectors be $E$, and the length of the target waypoint sequence be $L$. The solution to find is a whole-body joint trajectory of length $L$, $Q = (q_1, \dots, q_L)$.

The task specification is represented as a pair $T = (H, M)$, consisting of a target pose sequence $H \in \mathrm{SE}(3)^{L \times E}$ and boolean masks $M = (M_T, M_Q)$.
- $M_T$ is a target mask specifying "which target for which end-effector should be achieved."
- $M_Q$ is a configuration mask specifying "which joints or base coordinates the model should predict, and which should remain fixed as known."

This design is remarkably elegant. For example, setting $L=1$ recovers classical single-target IK, while $L>1$ enables trajectory IK. Enabling flags for both arms yields bimanual IK, and setting fixed flags for base coordinates yields fixed-base manipulator IK.

The goal is to rapidly sample diverse, preferred solutions from the feasible solution set $\mathcal{F}(R,T,S)$, where all active target poses are satisfied by the end-effectors (forward kinematics $\mathrm{FK}(q)$ error is below tolerance), joint limits are respected, and no collisions with the environment $S$ occur. During evaluation, a sample budget of $K$ solutions is generated to measure validity and Time To First Valid solution (TTFV).

sections.heading: Inside GenGenIK: Conditional Flow Matching and Flexible Guidance
sections.summary: Using bounded joint representations and canonical coordinate normalization, conditional Flow Matching learns a vector field from a Gaussian distribution to the solution distribution. It further incorporates test-time guidance via constraint tangent spaces, rollout fine-tuning to suppress collisions and self-intersections, and Reflow distillation for one-step inference.
sections.details:
### IV-A Data Generation and Feature Representation
Training data is generated at scale using cuRobo and verified with Drake's precise mesh collision checking. Joint angles pass through a custom soft bounding function $\mathcal{B}(\cdot)$ that smoothly saturates near limits, ensuring model predictions strictly stay within joint limits. Continuous rotational joints and mobile base yaw use a $(\cos q, \sin q)$ unit circle representation, and the entire coordinate frame is transformed into a canonical frame centered on the first target end-effector, ensuring geometric invariance to translations and yaw rotations.

### IV-B Conditional Flow Matching and Auxiliary Losses
The method adopts Flow Matching, which learns straighter and more efficient transport paths than diffusion models. It linearly interpolates between noise $Z$ and ground-truth solution $Y$, with the model $g_\theta$ predicting the residual toward the solution. In addition to the base velocity regression loss, the authors introduce a hinge visibility loss to keep end-effectors within the camera field of view, as well as a loss enforcing unit norms on rotation components.

### IV-C & IV-D Sampling and Rollout Training
At inference time, Euler integration with non-uniform time steps (Algorithm 2) generates solutions rapidly with few Function Evaluations (NFE). Furthermore, to reduce task-space errors and environmental penetrations caused by discretization steps, the authors perform fine-tuning by differentiating through the entire sampler rollout, backpropagating forward kinematics and signed distance field (SDF) collision penalties.

### IV-E & IV-F Reflow Distillation and Guidance Mechanism
To compress multi-step inference down to a single step, Reflow distillation is applied, training a 1-step student model using the inputs and outputs of the trained model as supervision.
During inference, gradient guidance via differentiable cost functions $E(Q)$—such as manipulability or static stability (center-of-mass margin from the support polygon)—is supported. To avoid breaking target end-effector constraints, gradients are projected onto the null space of the end-effector Jacobian (the constraint tangent space) and combined with damped Gauss-Newton corrections, steering toward preferred configurations while preserving IK precision.

### IV-G Conditional Transformer Architecture
The model uses an Encoder-Decoder Transformer architecture (Figure F2). The encoder processes task pose sequences, 32 environment point cloud tokens compressed by PointNet++, and non-differentiable behavioral prompts (e.g., "raise elbows"). The decoder updates solution tokens using self-attention, cross-attention, and AdaLN-Zero modulation. FK error vectors at each step are also provided as feedback inputs.

captions.F2: GenGenIK network architecture and sampling pipeline. Target end-effector poses, environment point clouds extracted by PointNet++, and behavioral prompts are packaged as conditioning tokens; the decoder receives FK residual feedback and iteratively updates noise into bounded joint trajectories.

sections.heading: Empirical Results: 34x Speedup, Obstacle Avoidance, and Trajectory Continuity
sections.summary: The authors evaluated free-space IK precision, obstacle avoidance in real-world kitchens and under partial point clouds, continuous mobile bimanual motions, and test-time guidance. GenGenIK significantly outperformed baselines like cuRobo in both success rate and speed, while showing zero-shot transfer to unseen task geometries.
sections.details:
### Basic Performance in Free Space
On free-space point IK across various single arms, dual arms, and humanoid robots (FR3, Panda, RB-Y1, G1, etc.), GenGenIK achieved position and rotation accuracy matching or exceeding IKFlow and IKDiffuser with very few network evaluations.

### Scene Awareness and Obstacle Avoidance (Table II)
Evaluations using the RB-Y1 robot in unseen household environments from iTHOR and ProcTHOR showed that even when fed partial point clouds from a single depth image, the collision rate dropped dramatically compared to the blind baseline without point clouds. Compared to GPU-parallelized cuRobo, GenGenIK achieved higher valid solution rates (S@K), especially in tightly constrained obstacle environments.

### Continuous Path IK and First-Pose Feasibility (Tables III, IV)
In path IK tasks completed with a stationary base—including door opening, drawer opening, pushing, bimanual lifting, and under-table picking—GenGenIK paired with a 1-step distilled model and a lightweight Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) refiner achieved up to a 34x speedup in Time To First Valid solution (TTFV) over cuRobo.
Even more crucial is the quality of the initial configuration. When conditioned on the entire path while solving the first waypoint, GenGenIK's initial poses allowed completing all subsequent motions without failure 58.2% of the time on average, more than double cuRobo (24.3%), which only considered the first point.

### Behavioral Preferences and Guidance (Figure F3, Table V)
Conditioning on non-differentiable prompt tokens—such as "keep base within 0.45m of target" or "keep right elbow high and left elbow low"—cleanly shifted the sampled distribution into the requested region (Figure F3). Additionally, on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, applying static stability guidance to prevent center-of-mass excursions outside the support polygon significantly lowered tipping violations while maintaining end-effector precision.

captions.F3: Preference conditioning results on the RB-Y1 bimanual lift task. In the left plot, requesting base proximity (within 0.45m) shifts the sampled distribution (blue points) forward toward the target object (black square) compared to unconditional sampling (gray points). In the right plot, specifying left and right elbow heights produces the intended asymmetric lifting posture.

sections.heading: Summary and What Lies Ahead
sections.summary: GenGenIK is a powerful framework that unifies generalized IK as a conditional generative model. It significantly surpasses optimization-based approaches in speed and success rate, with a single unified model matching task-specific models. Future work points toward broader generalization across unseen tasks.
sections.details:
This paper presented GenGenIK, a generative IK solver that handles mobile bases, multiple end-effectors, obstacle environments, and user preferences within a common interface.

In experiments, GenGenIK substantially outperformed numerical optimization methods in both solve rate and computation speed across manipulation tasks in unseen scenes. In particular, pairing the 1-step distilled model with a lightweight refiner achieved up to a 34x speedup compared to GPU-batched optimization.

Furthermore, a single unified model matched the performance of task-specific models and generalized to unseen trajectory lengths on certain tasks (pushing and flip-up). However, zero-shot generalization remains limited for qualitatively different geometric constraints, such as reaching under tables; expanding data collection across diverse interactions and building foundation models represent promising future directions.

takeaways: Switching the paradigm from "solving IK as a single point" to "rapidly sampling from a constraint-satisfying joint distribution" dramatically improves search efficiency in long-horizon planning.
Leveraging Transformer masking enables unified formulation of diverse IK tasks—single-target, bimanual, continuous trajectories, and partial joint fixing—within the same network.

A hybrid design combining test-time constrained optimization (tangent space projection guidance) with a lightweight LM refiner provides a highly practical fix for the slight precision gap typical of generative models.
limitations: Zero-shot extrapolation fails on qualitatively unseen geometric constraints not present in the training data (e.g., reaching into tight gaps or under tables), causing success rates to drop near 0%.
Because point clouds are compressed using PointNet++, resolution bottlenecks may arise when navigating extremely narrow gaps or resolving thin obstacles.
Generating the training data itself requires pre-computing tens to hundreds of thousands of heavy optimizations using tools like cuRobo, incurring onboarding costs for new robot morphologies.
